notes_list.title: Distance and Displacement
notes_list.basic_overview: Distance is the total path length travelled by an object, while displacement is the shortest directed distance between its initial and final positions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Distance is a scalar quantity, whereas displacement is a vector quantity. Displacement can be zero even when an object has travelled a non-zero distance.

notes_list.title: Speed and Velocity
notes_list.basic_overview: Speed describes the rate of change of distance, while velocity describes the rate of change of displacement.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Average speed equals total distance divided by total time. Average velocity equals total displacement divided by total time.

notes_list.title: Acceleration
notes_list.basic_overview: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The SI unit of acceleration is metre per second squared (m/s²). Acceleration may involve a change in speed, direction or both.

notes_list.title: Newton's First Law
notes_list.basic_overview: An object remains at rest or continues in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion is called inertia.

notes_list.title: Newton's Second Law
notes_list.basic_overview: The net force acting on an object is related to the rate of change of its momentum. For constant mass, this is commonly expressed as F = ma.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Force is measured in newtons. One newton is the force required to produce an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of 1 kg.

notes_list.title: Newton's Third Law
notes_list.basic_overview: When two bodies interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The action and reaction forces act on different bodies, so they do not simply cancel each other on a single free-body diagram.

notes_list.title: Work
notes_list.basic_overview: In physics, work is done when a force causes displacement of an object in the direction of the force or a component of it.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For a constant force, work can be calculated as W = F s cosθ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

notes_list.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy
notes_list.basic_overview: Kinetic energy is associated with motion, while potential energy is associated with position or configuration.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For translational motion, kinetic energy is KE = 1/2 mv². Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is approximately mgh.

notes_list.title: Power
notes_list.basic_overview: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The SI unit of power is watt. One watt equals one joule per second.

notes_list.title: Heat and Temperature
notes_list.basic_overview: Temperature indicates the thermal state of a system, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Temperature is measured using scales such as Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit. The SI unit of thermodynamic temperature is kelvin.

notes_list.title: Modes of Heat Transfer
notes_list.basic_overview: Heat can be transferred through conduction, convection and radiation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Conduction is dominant in solids, convection occurs through bulk movement of fluids, and radiation transfers energy through electromagnetic waves.

notes_list.title: Reflection of Light
notes_list.basic_overview: Reflection is the return of light into the original medium when it strikes a surface.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, with angles measured from the normal.

notes_list.title: Refraction of Light
notes_list.basic_overview: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes between media with different optical properties.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Snell's law relates the angles and refractive indices of the two media. The speed of light changes when light enters a different medium.

notes_list.title: Human Eye
notes_list.basic_overview: The human eye is an optical organ that forms images on the retina and converts light information into signals processed by the nervous system.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The cornea and lens focus light on the retina. The iris controls the amount of light entering through the pupil.

notes_list.title: Production and Propagation of Sound
notes_list.basic_overview: Sound is produced by vibrating sources and propagates through a material medium as mechanical waves.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Sound cannot propagate through vacuum. Its speed depends on the properties of the medium and temperature.

notes_list.title: Frequency and Pitch
notes_list.basic_overview: Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second, while pitch is the auditory perception primarily associated with frequency.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Frequency is measured in hertz. Human hearing is commonly described as approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, although the range varies between individuals.

notes_list.title: Electric Current
notes_list.basic_overview: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor or circuit.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The SI unit of current is ampere. Conventional current direction is taken from higher electric potential to lower potential in an external circuit.

notes_list.title: Ohm's Law
notes_list.basic_overview: For an ohmic conductor under constant physical conditions, current is proportional to potential difference, expressed as V = IR.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Resistance is measured in ohms. The relationship may change when physical conditions such as temperature change significantly.

notes_list.title: Electrical Power
notes_list.basic_overview: Electrical power is the rate of electrical energy transfer and can be expressed as P = VI.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Using Ohm's law, electrical power can also be expressed as P = I²R or P = V²/R for suitable circuit conditions.

notes_list.title: Magnetic Field
notes_list.basic_overview: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet, electric current or changing electric field in which magnetic effects can be observed.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Magnetic field direction can be represented using field lines. Outside a bar magnet, field lines conventionally run from north to south.

notes_list.title: Electromagnetic Induction
notes_list.basic_overview: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force when magnetic flux through a circuit changes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Faraday's law relates induced emf to the rate of change of magnetic flux. Generators use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.

notes_list.title: States of Matter
notes_list.basic_overview: Matter commonly exists as solids, liquids and gases, with different arrangements and motions of particles.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Solids have relatively fixed shape and volume, liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of their container, and gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.

notes_list.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
notes_list.basic_overview: A physical change generally changes the form or state of a substance without producing a new substance, while a chemical change produces one or more new substances.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Melting ice is a physical change, whereas rusting of iron is a chemical change.

notes_list.title: Atom
notes_list.basic_overview: An atom is the basic unit of an element that retains the chemical identity of that element.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Atoms contain a nucleus made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. The number of protons determines the atomic number of an element.

notes_list.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
notes_list.basic_overview: Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom, while mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons.

notes_list.title: Modern Periodic Table
notes_list.basic_overview: The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number and groups elements with related chemical properties.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The table contains periods and groups. Elements in the same group often show related valence-electron configurations and chemical behavior.

notes_list.title: Periodic Trends
notes_list.basic_overview: Properties such as atomic radius, ionization energy and electronegativity show systematic variations across periods and groups.
notes_list.extra_info_content: These trends arise largely from changes in nuclear charge, electron shielding and the distance of valence electrons from the nucleus.

notes_list.title: Chemical Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: A chemical reaction involves rearrangement of atoms and formation of new substances with different chemical properties.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common types include combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and combustion reactions.

notes_list.title: Oxidation and Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Oxidation and reduction are complementary processes involving transfer of electrons or changes in oxidation state.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Oxidation involves loss of electrons in the electron-transfer definition, while reduction involves gain of electrons.

notes_list.title: Acids and Bases
notes_list.basic_overview: Acids and bases are classes of substances with characteristic chemical properties. In aqueous systems, acids increase hydrogen ion concentration while bases increase hydroxide ion concentration under the Arrhenius definition.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The pH scale is commonly used to express acidity or basicity of aqueous solutions. A pH of 7 is neutral at 25°C under standard conditions.

notes_list.title: Salts
notes_list.basic_overview: Salts are ionic compounds that can be formed through reactions involving acids and bases among other chemical processes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common examples include sodium chloride, sodium carbonate and copper sulfate. The properties of salts depend on their constituent ions.

notes_list.title: Properties of Metals
notes_list.basic_overview: Metals generally show properties such as electrical and thermal conductivity, malleability and ductility, although exceptions exist.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Metals can form positive ions and often form ionic compounds with non-metals.

notes_list.title: Corrosion
notes_list.basic_overview: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a material, commonly a metal, due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with its environment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Rusting of iron requires suitable conditions involving oxygen and moisture. Painting, coating, alloying and other methods can help prevent corrosion.

notes_list.title: Carbon
notes_list.basic_overview: Carbon is a versatile element capable of forming stable covalent bonds and a very large number of compounds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Carbon's ability to form chains and rings is called catenation. It forms the basis of organic chemistry and many biological molecules.

notes_list.title: Hydrocarbons
notes_list.basic_overview: Hydrocarbons are compounds consisting only of carbon and hydrogen.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Hydrocarbons include alkanes, alkenes and alkynes. Their properties depend on molecular structure and bonding.

notes_list.title: Cell
notes_list.basic_overview: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cells may be broadly classified as prokaryotic or eukaryotic. Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles.

notes_list.title: Cell Organelles
notes_list.basic_overview: Cell organelles perform specialized functions necessary for cellular structure, metabolism and reproduction.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Important organelles include nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and, in plants, chloroplasts.

notes_list.title: Cell Division
notes_list.basic_overview: Cell division is the process through which cells reproduce and organisms grow, develop or repair tissues.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Mitosis generally produces genetically similar daughter cells, while meiosis produces haploid cells and contributes to genetic variation.

notes_list.title: Digestive System
notes_list.basic_overview: The digestive system breaks food into smaller molecules that can be absorbed and used by the body.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Major organs include the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The liver and pancreas provide important digestive secretions.

notes_list.title: Respiratory System
notes_list.basic_overview: The respiratory system enables exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the body and the external environment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Gas exchange occurs mainly across the thin walls of alveoli in the lungs.

notes_list.title: Circulatory System
notes_list.basic_overview: The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and other substances through the body and helps remove metabolic wastes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The human cardiovascular system consists primarily of the heart, blood and blood vessels. The heart maintains blood circulation through pulmonary and systemic circuits.

notes_list.title: Nervous System
notes_list.basic_overview: The nervous system receives information, processes signals and coordinates responses throughout the body.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the peripheral nervous system connects the central system with the rest of the body.

notes_list.title: Photosynthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and certain other organisms use light energy to synthesize organic compounds from carbon dioxide and water.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In oxygenic photosynthesis, oxygen is released as a by-product. Chlorophyll and other pigments absorb light energy.

notes_list.title: Plant Respiration
notes_list.basic_overview: Plant cells carry out cellular respiration to release usable energy from organic molecules.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cellular respiration occurs in both plants and animals. Aerobic respiration primarily occurs in mitochondria after the initial stages of glucose breakdown.

notes_list.title: Plant Transport
notes_list.basic_overview: Plants transport water, minerals and organic nutrients through specialized vascular tissues.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Xylem mainly transports water and mineral ions, while phloem transports sugars and other organic substances.

notes_list.title: DNA
notes_list.basic_overview: DNA is the primary hereditary material in most organisms and stores genetic information used in cellular processes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: DNA is composed of nucleotides containing a sugar, phosphate group and nitrogenous base. The bases include adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine.

notes_list.title: Genes and Chromosomes
notes_list.basic_overview: Genes are functional units of hereditary information located at specific positions on chromosomes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Chromosomes are structures containing DNA and associated proteins. Humans normally have 46 chromosomes in somatic cells.

notes_list.title: Mendelian Genetics
notes_list.basic_overview: Mendelian genetics describes patterns of inheritance based on principles derived from Gregor Mendel's experiments with pea plants.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Important concepts include alleles, dominance, segregation and independent assortment, although many traits involve more complex inheritance patterns.

notes_list.title: Infectious Diseases
notes_list.basic_overview: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogenic organisms or agents such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa or parasitic organisms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Transmission may occur through air, contaminated food or water, direct contact, vectors or other routes depending on the disease.

notes_list.title: Immunity
notes_list.basic_overview: Immunity is the ability of an organism to recognize and respond to harmful foreign substances or pathogens.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The immune system includes innate and adaptive components. Adaptive immunity involves specialized lymphocytes and immunological memory.

notes_list.title: Vaccination
notes_list.basic_overview: Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize specific pathogens or their components and can provide protection against infectious diseases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Vaccines can stimulate immune memory without requiring the individual to experience the full disease.

notes_list.title: Ecosystem
notes_list.basic_overview: An ecosystem consists of living organisms interacting with one another and with the non-living components of their environment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Biotic components include producers, consumers and decomposers, while abiotic components include factors such as light, temperature, water and soil.

notes_list.title: Food Chain and Food Web
notes_list.basic_overview: A food chain represents a sequence of feeding relationships, while a food web represents interconnected food chains within an ecosystem.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Energy generally flows from producers to consumers and decomposers, with substantial energy dissipation at each trophic transfer.

notes_list.title: Biodiversity
notes_list.basic_overview: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Biodiversity contributes to ecosystem functioning, ecological resilience and the provision of ecosystem services.

notes_list.title: Evolution
notes_list.basic_overview: Biological evolution refers to changes in heritable characteristics of populations across generations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Evolution can occur through mechanisms including natural selection, mutation, genetic drift and gene flow.

notes_list.title: Natural Selection
notes_list.basic_overview: Natural selection occurs when heritable variations affect survival or reproductive success, causing some traits to become more common across generations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Natural selection acts on existing heritable variation; populations, rather than individual organisms, evolve across generations.

notes_list.title: Layers of Earth
notes_list.basic_overview: Earth has major internal layers including the crust, mantle and core, each with distinct physical and chemical characteristics.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The core is predominantly metallic and is divided into an outer liquid core and inner solid core. The mantle lies between the crust and core.

notes_list.title: Plate Tectonics
notes_list.basic_overview: Plate tectonics describes the large-scale movement of rigid lithospheric plates over the Earth's asthenosphere.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Plate interactions contribute to earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building and the formation of many geological features.

notes_list.title: Composition of Atmosphere
notes_list.basic_overview: Earth's atmosphere is primarily composed of nitrogen and oxygen, along with smaller amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Atmospheric composition varies with altitude, location and environmental conditions, particularly for water vapour and aerosols.

notes_list.title: Ozone Layer
notes_list.basic_overview: The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere containing relatively high concentrations of ozone that absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Certain human-produced ozone-depleting substances can cause stratospheric ozone depletion. International agreements have addressed many of these substances.

notes_list.title: Weather and Climate
notes_list.basic_overview: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions, whereas climate describes long-term patterns and averages of weather over an extended period.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure are important elements used to describe weather and climate.

notes_list.title: Greenhouse Effect
notes_list.basic_overview: The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth's lower atmosphere and surface caused by absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared radiation by greenhouse gases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are among the important greenhouse gases. Human activities have increased concentrations of several greenhouse gases.

notes_list.title: Air Pollution
notes_list.basic_overview: Air pollution occurs when harmful substances or pollutants are present in the atmosphere at concentrations that can cause adverse effects.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Important pollutants include particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide and ground-level ozone.

notes_list.title: Water Pollution
notes_list.basic_overview: Water pollution occurs when physical, chemical or biological contaminants degrade water quality.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Sources may include untreated sewage, industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, plastics and other contaminants.

notes_list.title: Renewable and Non-renewable Resources
notes_list.basic_overview: Renewable resources can naturally replenish on human-relevant timescales under appropriate conditions, while non-renewable resources are finite on such timescales.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Solar energy, wind energy and sustainably managed biomass are examples of renewable resources. Coal, petroleum and many mineral deposits are non-renewable.

notes_list.title: Water Conservation
notes_list.basic_overview: Water conservation involves reducing unnecessary consumption, improving efficiency, protecting water sources and supporting sustainable water management.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation, wastewater treatment and watershed management are among the approaches used for water conservation.

notes_list.title: Earthquake
notes_list.basic_overview: An earthquake is the shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the sudden release of energy within the Earth, commonly associated with movement along faults.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Earthquake magnitude describes the size of the seismic event, while intensity describes observed effects at a particular location.

notes_list.title: Cyclone
notes_list.basic_overview: A tropical cyclone is a rotating low-pressure weather system that forms over sufficiently warm tropical or subtropical waters under suitable atmospheric conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Tropical cyclones can produce strong winds, heavy rainfall, storm surges and flooding.

notes_list.title: The Solar System
notes_list.basic_overview: The Solar System consists of the Sun and the objects gravitationally bound to it, including planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

notes_list.title: Earth and Moon
notes_list.basic_overview: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and has one natural satellite, the Moon.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Moon's phases result from changing viewing geometry as the Moon orbits Earth. Its gravitational interaction with Earth contributes strongly to ocean tides.

notes_list.title: Stars
notes_list.basic_overview: Stars are massive, gravitationally bound bodies of plasma that produce energy through nuclear processes in their interiors.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Sun is a star. Stellar colour and spectra provide information about temperature, composition and other physical properties.

notes_list.title: Life Cycle of Stars
notes_list.basic_overview: Stars undergo different evolutionary stages depending largely on their initial mass.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Massive stars may end as supernovae and leave behind neutron stars or black holes, while lower-mass stars can evolve through red giant and white dwarf stages.

notes_list.title: Galaxy
notes_list.basic_overview: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system containing stars, gas, dust, dark matter and other components.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Galaxies can have different forms, including spiral, elliptical and irregular structures.

notes_list.title: Milky Way
notes_list.basic_overview: The Milky Way is the galaxy containing the Solar System.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Solar System lies in one of the Milky Way's spiral-arm regions, at a substantial distance from the galactic centre.

notes_list.title: ISRO
notes_list.basic_overview: The Indian Space Research Organisation is India's national space agency responsible for developing and operating a wide range of space and satellite technologies and missions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Indian space activities include launch vehicles, Earth observation, communication satellites, navigation systems, planetary exploration and space science missions.

notes_list.title: Chandrayaan Programme
notes_list.basic_overview: The Chandrayaan programme consists of Indian lunar exploration missions designed to study the Moon using spacecraft and scientific instruments.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Chandrayaan-1 contributed to the detection of evidence associated with water/hydroxyl on the lunar surface, while later missions expanded India's lunar exploration capabilities.

notes_list.title: Mars Orbiter Mission
notes_list.basic_overview: India's Mars Orbiter Mission, also known as Mangalyaan, was India's first interplanetary mission and entered Mars orbit in 2014.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The mission demonstrated India's capability in deep-space navigation, communication and spacecraft operations around another planet.

notes_list.title: Artificial Satellites
notes_list.basic_overview: Artificial satellites are human-made objects placed into orbit around Earth or other celestial bodies for scientific, communication, navigation, observation and other purposes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Satellite orbits are selected according to mission requirements. Geostationary and polar orbits serve different applications.

notes_list.title: Carbohydrates
notes_list.basic_overview: Carbohydrates are biomolecules that serve important roles as energy sources and structural components in living organisms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Glucose is an important carbohydrate used in cellular respiration. Complex carbohydrates include starch and dietary fibre.

notes_list.title: Proteins
notes_list.basic_overview: Proteins are polymers of amino acids that perform structural, catalytic, transport, regulatory and many other functions in living organisms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Enzymes are mostly proteins and act as biological catalysts. Dietary proteins provide amino acids required for growth and maintenance.

notes_list.title: Vitamins and Minerals
notes_list.basic_overview: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients required in relatively small amounts for normal physiological functions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Different vitamins and minerals have distinct biological functions. Both deficiency and excessive intake of some nutrients can cause health problems.

notes_list.title: Plastics
notes_list.basic_overview: Plastics are polymeric materials that can be molded into a wide variety of forms and are used in numerous applications.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Different plastics have different properties. Their environmental impacts depend on production, use, disposal and recycling practices.

notes_list.title: Alloys
notes_list.basic_overview: An alloy is a material containing two or more elements, at least one of which is typically a metal, designed to obtain useful properties.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include steel, stainless steel, brass and bronze. Alloying can modify strength, hardness, corrosion resistance and other properties.

notes_list.title: Renewable Energy
notes_list.basic_overview: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sunlight, wind, flowing water and geothermal heat.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Solar photovoltaic systems convert light directly into electricity, while wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy.

notes_list.title: Electric Vehicles
notes_list.basic_overview: Electric vehicles use electric motors for propulsion and generally store electrical energy in rechargeable batteries.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Electric drivetrains can convert electrical energy into mechanical motion efficiently, while overall environmental impact depends on factors including electricity generation and battery production.

notes_list.title: Electromagnetic Communication
notes_list.basic_overview: Modern wireless communication uses electromagnetic waves to transmit information through space or other media.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Different communication systems use different frequency ranges, modulation techniques, antennas and signal-processing methods.

notes_list.title: Optical Fibre
notes_list.basic_overview: Optical fibre transmits information as pulses of light through thin strands of glass or other suitable materials.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Total internal reflection enables light to remain guided within the fibre. Optical fibre supports high-bandwidth communication over long distances.
